newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma students thwarted by tight Rangoon security.
newsitem.headline: Burma students thwarted by tight Rangoon security.

text.p: Burma boosted security around Rangoon's city hall on Thursday to prevent a rumoured demonstration, part of a crackdown which diplomats said may force student protesters to shift to the provinces.

The military, responding to rumours that university students may attempt a demonstration in a square in front of city hall in Rangoon's business district, placed about 20 truckloads of soldiers and riot police at the site.
Protesters, however, failed to show up at the square, which was fronted by military trucks, but no soldiers.

"Both the government and students are running against time. The authorities are using tough measures to try to stifle protests as quickly as possible while students are struggling to keep the momentum of their activities," a Rangoon-based diplomat told Reuters.
The Sule Pagoda, a landmark in the central district adjoining the square, was closed, apparently as part of security measures.
The government has also postponed the Rangoon Mayor Marathon, which had been scheduled for Saturday.

The annual event, which attracts thousands of Burmese and foreign participants, was to be run on thoroughfares that have since been blockaded bordering the closed Yangon (Rangoon) University and the Yangon Institute of Technology.

Students from the two universities last week led the biggest street protests seen in Rangoon since the 1988 pro-democracy uprisings that were crushed by the military, leaving thousands dead or in jail.
In the latest protests demanding more politicial freedom, more than 860 people were detained and later freed by the government.
"Although student protests have slowed down, security has not been eased. In fact, the roadblock network seems to have been gradually widened," another diplomat said.
Due to the widening security net, protesters could be forced to take their demonstrations to the countryside, diplomats added.
Sporadic student rallies have occurred in recent days outside the capital. Witnesses said about 200 students protested in the eastern town of Pa-an and were forcibly dispersed by police.

Another diplomat said students in the eastern town of Mawlamyine in Mon State might protest next. Student sources said universities could be shut for at least a month. The student protesters have also demanded that their colleges not be closed, remembering that universities were closed for more than two years after the 1988 uprising.

A diplomat said he had detected no signs that the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) would ease its tough stand against the students. The students were also expected to keep pushing, he added.
"I think protests will not disappear until the government addresses student grievances," the diplomat said.
Most diplomats said they did not expect an anti-government alliance soon between the students and opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her National League for Democracy (NLD).
"It is basically a student problem. I still don't see any poltical motive or tactical reason for the NLD to get involved," a diplomat said.
A government spokesman this week accused some NLD members and elements of exiled Burmese students and the outlawed Communist Party of Burma of instigating student protests.
